Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas brings together Alabama and Coushatta people in a shared East Texas government. Its own history and a dated constitutional text provide starting points for understanding the community, its institutions and its continuing relationship with the Big Thicket. Broader Alabama and Coushatta routes remain separately available.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Two peoples and a shared Texas history

The Tribe’s historical account distinguishes Alabama and Coushatta people before describing their movement into East Texas and their relationships with successive governments. Its timeline includes federal restoration in 1987. Read this as the Tribe’s institutional synthesis: the narrative’s treaty and land-title statements need comparison with the actual instruments, and the page’s undated population figures are not used as current facts.

Read the sources [2] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

02

Reading a governing document

The hosted Constitution and By-Laws provides a different kind of evidence. The previously inspected preamble and selected provisions describe the government’s name, organization, chiefs, council, powers and courts. This is a dated revised and annotated document, not a guarantee that every provision is the current consolidated rule. Keeping it beside community history helps distinguish a published institutional narrative from a governing instrument.

Read the sources [3] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

03

Place without a boundary claim

The Tribe’s history places this Texas community in the Big Thicket. The credited cypress photograph supplies regional environmental context. It shows a national-preserve landscape, not the Tribe’s reservation boundary, a named family’s property or a cultural site. Alabama and Coushatta communities elsewhere should be read through their own sources.
